instructions: The day before, or at least 3 hours ahead: pat the pork hocks dry. Heat the oil in a large heavy pot over medium-high heat. Brown the hocks on all sides for about 8 minutes, until deep golden. Stand back a little, they will spatter. Transfer them to a plate.
Finely chop 3 of the garlic cloves with the stems from the cilantro and the peppercorns, then pound or mash them into a rough paste. Keep the cilantro leaves for the table.
Lower the heat to medium. Add the paste, cinnamon sticks, star anise and shiitake to the same pot and stir for 1 minute, until it smells fragrant.
Add 1/4 cup of the brown sugar and stir for 1 minute, until it begins to melt and darken.
Add 6 cups water, the soy sauce, dark soy sauce, five spice powder and salt and stir. Return the pork and any juices to the pot and bring to a boil.
Lower the heat, cover and cook for 2 1/2 hours, turning the pork once or twice, until the meat is tender and a fork slides into it with no resistance. The skin should be soft.
About 45 minutes before the pork is done, cover the eggs with cold water in a small pot and bring to a boil. Boil for 10 minutes, then cool them in cold water and peel them.
Add the eggs to the braising liquid for the last 30 minutes.
If the pork was cooked earlier, reheat it in its liquid over low heat, covered, for 15 minutes, until hot.
Meanwhile, rinse the rice, add it to a pot with 2 1/4 cups water and bring to a boil. Cover and cook over low heat for 15 minutes, then leave it covered off the heat for 5 minutes.
Make the chili vinegar sauce: finely chop the chilies and the remaining 2 garlic cloves. Stir them in a small bowl with the rice vinegar, the remaining 1/2 tsp brown sugar and a pinch of salt.
Cut the Chinese broccoli into 2 inch pieces and blanch them in boiling water for 2 minutes, until just tender. Drain. Slice the pickled mustard greens.
Slice the pork off the bone. Spoon the rice into bowls and top with the pork, a halved egg, the broccoli and the mustard greens. Spoon some of the braising liquid over the rice.

Serve with the chili vinegar sauce and a few cilantro leaves. Keep leftover pork in its liquid in the fridge for up to 3 days, or in the freezer for up to 3 months, and reheat it gently as in the reheat step above.
advance_prep_notes: Braise the pork the day before or at least 3 hours ahead. It keeps and tastes better the next day.
method_notes: Hungry in Thailand leads (5 from 4 votes): pork leg browned, then braised for hours in a paste of garlic, cilantro root and peppercorns with cinnamon, star anise, shiitake, five spice, light and dark soy and palm sugar. Asian Inspirations braises for 1.5 to 2 hours, adds galangal and serves a chili vinegar sauce, which is used here. Changed for the list: pork hocks stand in for the pork leg, brown sugar replaces palm sugar, and the greens and pickled mustard come from Asian Inspirations. Under 20 ratings, so this is a fallback lead.
